So Mary, what can we expect to see?
Well, it's such an exciting time to be in Yorktown. To kick off the Spring Festival,

Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
First, a bit of background. In recent years people have been trying to exploit a number
of different renewable forms of energy. One of these is wind power.
Electricity can be generated from wind power by turbines, and at present large numbers
of these tall wind turbines are being erected in what are called wind farms. And the government
is backing these as part of its moves towards sustainable energy production. But wind farms
can be a problem for birds, because they can fly into the turbines and injure themselves.
So wildlife experts have been doing a number of studies recently trying to monitor the
effects of wind farms on bird populations and suggest solutions, and that's what I'm
going to look at today. Now before I look in detail at specific
studies of different birds, I want to make some general points. It has been established that the
species in greatest danger from the turbines are those which, irrespective of their feeding or
patterns of migration, collect together in significant numbers, either on the coast or in
land. And as well as that, birds are often vulnerable when they're setting off on long
sea migrations, or when they're flying below cloud. So in my opinion, efforts should be
made to site new wind farms responsibly, and that means avoiding low lying areas and narrow
valleys between mountains or hills. Now I'd like to look at some specific studies. Firstly,
a project looking at one particular species of bird, the vulture. This investigation
mainly focused on how high the birds fly and the correlation between this and
weather conditions. One of the weather features they were looking at was wind
speed but as well as that another thing they considered to do with the weather
was the amount of cloud. Now what emerged from this study was that these
vultures tend to fly lower at times when the wind is very strong and of
course this means that more birds are in danger of flying straight into the
turbines. Now the project team suggests that to deal with this problem a fixed camera should
be set up to film any birds in flight near the turbines so that if necessary the turbines
can be switched off. Another survey looked at the night time or nocturnal habits of
several species of birds. This study actually had a slightly wider scope. It looked at
risks to these birds near other installations, not just wind farms. These were mainly airports,
which for obvious reasons tend to cause problems for birds. But the study also looked at what
happened near tall structures, such as radio transmitters. In the past, the most usual
means of tracking the movements of birds at night were radar and thermal imaging. Now
But the problem was that these methods were expensive because someone had to control the
devices all through the night.
And in addition to this, they weren't really reliable.
So the researchers looked for an alternative that didn't need human intervention.
And what they proposed as a priority was to create alarm systems that switch on whenever
a bird passes a certain point, alerting monitors so that action can be taken.
And then, their second proposal was that findings should be processed to generate computer models,
which can be used by wind farm planners and anyone else with an interest in reducing the
number of collisions.
